episodes.yt: How Marie Antoinette Became the Symbol of Everything France Hated
episodes.u: Opening their French Revolution series, the hosts explore why Marie Antoinette became the focus of hatred for the old regime, from her Habsburg birth and diplomatic marriage to her lonely first years at Versailles. They weigh her mismatched marriage to Louis XVI, her Trianon retreat and fashion revolution, and the court-bred slanders that lead toward the Diamond Necklace affair.

g.u: The hosts launch their first French Revolution series, outlining its scope from the causes through the Bastille to the royal family's failed escape.
Why Marie Antoinette became the emblem of royal arrogance and excess for revolutionaries, and why the famous cake remark is a myth.
The rival conservative image of the queen as tragic victim, from Edmund Burke's 1790 Reflections to the sympathetic tone of most modern biographers.
Screen portrayals, from the film of Chantal Thomas's novel to Sofia Coppola's 2006 biopic, whose split Cannes reception mirrors French divisions over the queen.
Before 1789 she was already both admired and loathed; the hosts cast her as a fashion-setting modern queen and the Revolution as competing narratives.
Born a Habsburg in 1755, she embodied the Diplomatic Revolution, as Prussian and British power pushed old enemies Austria and France into alliance.
Choiseul, French envoy in Vienna, conceives a match between Maria Theresa's youngest daughter and Louis XV's grandson, sealed by a 1770 proxy wedding and departure.
r: e:n:proxy wedding of marie antoinette in vienna

g.u: French hostility to Austria dogs her as l'Autrichienne, despite her Lorraine-born father; she is cast as Maria Theresa's agent sent to undermine France.
Her preparation under tutor Abbé de Vermond reveals a scanty education and light temperament, though observers praise her charm, complexion and poise.
At a pavilion on a Rhine island the 14-year-old is stripped of Austrian dress and handed to the Comtesse de Noailles, her etiquette mistress.
r: e:n:handover of marie antoinette on the rhine
l:n:rhine island pavilion near strasbourg and kehl

g.u: She meets the Dauphin and Louis XV near Compiègne and marries; a deadly crush at the celebration fireworks in Paris is read as an omen.
r: e:n:wedding of louis xvi and marie antoinette
e:n:fireworks disaster at the place louis xv (1770)

g.u: France as a demographic and cultural giant, and Versailles as the monumental expression of the absolutism Louis XIV built by taming the nobility.
Isolated at a factional court after Choiseul's fall, she faces hostile royal aunts and an envious Comte de Provence, yet already chafes at etiquette.
r: e:n:dismissal of the duc de choiseul

g.u: Shocked by Louis XV's mistress Madame du Barry, the dauphine snubs her until Maria Theresa, needing French support over Poland, forces one grudging remark.
Louis XV dies of smallpox in 1774 amid lurid rumours; the hosts stress how court factions fed public gossip; the young couple take the throne.
r: e:n:death of louis xv and accession of louis xvi

g.u: Whether Louis XVI was dominated by his wife, and their musical mismatch: she played and had met the young Mozart, he disdained the arts.
Her pug Mops is restored to her; Louis shoots cats on Versailles roofs, adores hunting and logs kills tersely, explaining his 14 July 1789 entry.
Awkward on foot and in society, Louis prefers ships, harbours and his locksmith's workshop; the hosts warmly recommend Simon Schama's Citizens.
Provence feeds pamphleteers mocking the king; the marriage goes unconsummated for seven years, with phimosis long debated and now doubted as the cause.
Royal heirs being a state matter, Joseph II visits in 1777 and reports on the couple's failure; Louis emerges as decent and diligent but unimpressive.
r: e:n:visit of joseph ii to france (1777)

g.u: The couple eventually have four children and grow devoted; Louis takes no mistress, exiles Madame du Barry and gives the Petit Trianon to his queen.
At the Trianon she indulges Rousseau-inspired ideals of nature and simplicity, visits his tomb, and builds a model hamlet that only the Revolution made notorious.
Her charity, such as housing poor families at the Trianon and having her children forgo toys for the needy, is likened to modern celebrity philanthropy.
With dressmaker Rose Bertin she swaps stiff court silks and corsets for loose white muslin, pioneering the self-chosen style behind France's fashion reputation.
Her hairdresser Léonard creates towering poufs and nature-themed styles, then, as her hair thins in 1781, a short childlike cut that sweeps Europe.
Her inner circle, notably the Duchesse de Polignac and the impressionable Princesse de Lamballe, compared to a teen-film clique, and the rumours it attracted.
The Swedish officer Axel von Fersen, met at an Opera masked ball in 1774, becomes a close friend; the hosts doubt they were lovers.
Joseph II faults her disregard for royal decorum; living like a favourite at the Trianon, she attracts mistress-style slanders of greed and promiscuity from 1774.
The libertine culture seen in Laclos and Sade shapes pornographic pamphlets about her that endanger the monarchy, leading into the Diamond Necklace affair.
Closing sign-off ahead of the next episode on the Diamond Necklace affair.

episodes.yt: The Scandal That Made France Turn on Marie Antoinette
episodes.u: Starting from Beaumarchais's scandalous 1784 comedy The Marriage of Figaro, the hosts recount the Affair of the Diamond Necklace, in which the con artist Jeanne de la Motte tricked Cardinal de Rohan into buying a huge necklace supposedly for Marie Antoinette. They then show how the open trials and the libels that followed wrecked the standing of the queen and Louis XVI in the years before 1789.

g.u: The hosts introduce the diamond necklace scandal and explain why they open with Beaumarchais's comedy The Marriage of Figaro.
A walk through the plot of The Marriage of Figaro: a lecherous count, swapped disguises in a night garden, and a closing reconciliation.
Why the 1784 comedy was seen as subversive, and how Louis XVI's attempts to ban it held up its staging for three years.
r: e:n:premiere of the marriage of figaro

g.u: Beaumarchais's colorful career: royal secret agent in London, contacts with the Chevalier d'Éon, arms supplier to the Americans and publisher of Voltaire.
Court factions, including Marie Antoinette and the Comte d'Artois, back the play, which becomes a sensation as nobles applaud satire aimed at themselves.
r: e:n:premiere of the marriage of figaro

g.u: In August 1784 a Paris milliner who resembles the queen is lured to Versailles, given an invented title, and dressed in the queen's signature style.
At midnight in the Versailles gardens the impostor gives a rose to a cloaked man, is hurried away, and later shown a forged thank-you note.
The cloaked man was Cardinal Louis de Rohan, a proud, credulous grandee who had earned the queen's hatred by mocking her mother from Vienna.
Claiming Valois descent, Jeanne de la Motte becomes the cardinal's protégée and likely lover, wins rooms at Versailles, and poses as the queen's friend.
The necklace: 647 diamonds made by Boehmer and Bassenge for Madame du Barry, unsold after Louis XV died, and wholly unsuited to Marie Antoinette's taste.
The occultist Cagliostro, a charlatan of murky Italian origins peddling Egyptian Freemasonry, befriends Rohan in Strasbourg in 1781 and may have fed the delusion.
Duped by a forged letter, Rohan buys the necklace on credit and gives it to a bogus courier; its diamonds end up sold in London.
Unpaid jewelers alert the queen, the fraud unravels, and on 15 August 1785 Rohan is arrested in vestments at Versailles and taken to the Bastille.
Why a necklace mattered: open trials, lawyers' trial briefs selling in vast numbers and read aloud in cafés made the affair a national obsession.
A modern parallel: the hosts liken the public frenzy to the collapse of the marriage of Prince Charles and Princess Diana.
Rohan lives comfortably in the Bastille, is tried by the Parlement of Paris as a naive dupe, and his acquittal humiliates the queen.
Nicole wins sympathy after giving birth in the Bastille, while Cagliostro swaps mystical boasts for Enlightenment reason at trial and is cleared.
Jeanne de la Motte, convicted and insisting the queen was guilty, is flogged, branded with a V and confined for life in the Salpêtrière.
Jeanne escapes in 1787 to London and publishes lurid claims of a lesbian affair with the queen, casting herself as a persecuted innocent.
r: e:n:escape of jeanne de la motte

g.u: Though the queen's own morals were conventional, the scandal magnified and publicized smears of her as insatiable, feeding obscene pamphlets by 1789.
The smears spread to her favorites Polignac and Lamballe, inspire fantasies of public punishment, and add charges of incest with Joseph II and Austrian treason.
A 1775 letter shows the queen scorning the libels, but from 1785 Paris crowds turn cold, then hostile, and she retreats to the Petit Trianon.
The affair also tars Louis XVI as a despot; the hosts note his milder jailing of Beaumarchais at Saint-Lazare and argue he was no tyrant.
Louis is also mocked as impotent and cuckolded, while Jeanne's London memoir alleges a queen-cardinal plot to subordinate France to Austria.
Amid fiscal crisis and hunger the slanders gained force; the hosts note they came from within the elite, notably Provence and Orléans's Palais-Royal pamphleteers.
Preview of the next episodes: the crisis of the 1780s, the calling of the Estates-General, the Tennis Court Oath and the fall of the Bastille.

episodes.yt: The French Revolution: The Violence Begins
episodes.u: The hosts trace how royal debt, swollen by the American war, drove Calonne and then Brienne into confrontations with the notables and the parlements that wrecked royal authority in 1786-1788. The story ends with the Day of the Tiles in Grenoble, the Vizille assembly and the monarchy's bankruptcy in August 1788.

g.u: The hosts frame the Revolution as the defining event of modern history, noting its symbols, the left-right divide and the great writers it inspired.
A simple three-part explanation of the Revolution: royal bankruptcy, hunger after freak weather, and a utopian culture of virtue; plus historians' return to narrative.
After recalling the necklace scandal, the hosts introduce Louis XVI, king at nineteen in 1774, and the populous, wealthy, regionally diverse realm he inherited.
Louis's nominally absolute power rests on judges, nobles and intendants amid an unmappable tangle of customs; he is an Enlightenment tinkerer who respects subjects' rights.
Far from the decrepit regime of Dickens, late eighteenth-century France buzzed with innovation: chemistry, a ballooning craze from 1783, and adulation of Benjamin Franklin.
The hosts weigh whether the American republic inspired France, seeing shared vocabulary rather than direct cause, and note Louis backed rebels chiefly to wound Britain.
Rapid change created losers such as displaced artisans, while Paris grew a lively political culture of cafés, street-corner pamphlets and newly named public opinion.
A younger romantic generation devoted to Rousseau, Marie Antoinette among them, prized sincere feeling and tears over the ironic scepticism of Voltaire's age.
Virtue becomes an unchallengeable, rather masculine ideal later personified by Robespierre, in a country already used to riots, lynchings and brutal public executions.
France's money troubles: costly global wars, a richer British rival, debts since the 1720s, no national bank after John Law's crash, and crushing interest payments.
Lacking a tax-voting parliament like Britain's, France had only the long-dormant Estates General and relied on patchy levies, the salt tax and internal customs barriers.
Turgot's free-market reforms, including freeing the grain trade, bring price rises and looting; Louis drops him, typical of a king who retreats under pressure.
Necker bankrolls French entry into the American war with short-term loans; hoped-for Caribbean gains never arrive, leaving huge debts and a fatally weakened monarchy.
In August 1786 Calonne warns Louis of a huge deficit and maturing war loans, but reform runs into nobles' and clergy's cherished exemption from taxation.
The parlements, high courts that must register royal edicts, had resisted new taxes since the 1750s, posing as guardians of liberty against royal despotism.
Louis seldom leaves Versailles, a journey ordinary Parisians cannot afford, feeding an image of a stuffy, isolated court set against a politically lively capital.
To get around the parlements, Calonne persuades a hesitant Louis to summon an Assembly of Notables, a step Popkin sees as starting the monarchy's undoing.
Calonne asks the notables for a universal land tax, freer internal trade and provincial assemblies; they refuse, insisting only the Estates General could approve taxes.
Calonne appeals to the public with a pamphlet read in churches and markets; the furious notables get him sacked, and public opinion sides with them.
r: e:n:dismissal of charles alexandre de calonne

g.u: New minister Loménie de Brienne, a worldly archbishop with a disfiguring skin disease, finds the deficit even worse; the notables refuse again and are dissolved.
A gloomy, increasingly obese Louis and Brienne weigh two bad options: summon the unpredictable Estates General or force the taxes through the parlements.
The Parlement of Paris rejects Brienne's taxes in novel language of consent and citizens, while liberal nobles like Orléans genuinely want a British-style constitution.
r: e:n:parlement of paris refuses to register the stamp and land taxes

g.u: Brienne banishes the Parlement to Troyes, sparking violent riots in Paris; troops patrol the streets, clubs are closed and the crown struggles to keep order.
r: e:n:exile of the parlement of paris to troyes

g.u: Brienne's 1788 scheme to strip the parlements of power through a new plenary court sparks riots, fiercest in provincial capitals proud of their own courts.
Grenoble, capital of Dauphiné, is pitched as the Revolution's real birthplace: an ordinary provincial town dependent on its parlement and hit by a glove-trade slump.
On 7 June 1788 Grenoble rises against troops sent to remove its judges; tiles rain from rooftops, soldiers fire, and rioters take over the town.
Ambitious young judge Jean-Joseph Mounier calls the Vizille assembly, which demands provincial estates, a doubled Third Estate and voting together in a single chamber.
Vizille's rhetoric brands opponents traitors, and writers like Volney and d'Antraigues reject precedent for natural rights and popular sovereignty, starker than British or American models.
Brienne convinces a fearful Louis to summon the Estates General, announced in August 1788, and soon afterwards concedes the treasury is empty.
A cliffhanger on France's bankruptcy, a preview of the Estates General meeting in the next episode, and a plug for the show's paid club.

episodes.yt: The Moment the French Revolution Became Unstoppable
episodes.u: From the hailstorm and brutal winter of 1788-89 through bread shortages, the Réveillon riots and the opening of the Estates General, the hosts trace how economic misery and political deadlock fed each other. The Third Estate proclaims itself the National Assembly, swears the Tennis Court Oath and forces Louis XVI to yield, before the king's dismissal of Necker on 11 July 1789 sets up the crisis in Paris.

g.u: A violent hailstorm, then drought and heat, devastate French farms in 1788; church, crown and a lottery raise relief money that falls far short.
Recap of the Dauphiné revolt and the summoning of the Estates General; Brienne's partial bankruptcy leads to his fall and Necker's return.
The hosts liken Necker's reputation as a sober foreign saviour to how Britons viewed Canadian central banker Mark Carney at the Bank of England.
Necker secures loans through banking friends and calms the markets, but the ruined harvest looms and Paris celebrations turn into deadly clashes with the watch.
How a laborer's wages compare with the cost of the standard four-pound loaf, why rising bread prices spell disaster, and how rumors blame hoarding ministers.
An early, savage winter freezes the Seine and the mills, blocks roads, and threatens landless laborers and indebted sharecroppers with starvation and eviction.
Rural migrants find little in the cities, where cheap British imports under Calonne's trade treaty already cost jobs and a fifth of Paris needs relief.
With no precedent since 1614, pamphleteers argue over the Estates General's form, reformers demanding a doubled Third Estate and voting by head in one body.
Abbé Sieyès's pamphlet What Is the Third Estate? casts commoners as the whole nation and the privileged orders as a disease on it.
Necker and the king double the Third Estate to 600 deputies, open it to nobles and clergy, but leave voting undecided; tiered elections follow.
r: e:n:elections to the estates general of 1789

g.u: The king invites grievances, and some 25,000 cahiers pour in, an unprecedented survey that stokes contradictory hopes no government could satisfy.
As the thaw comes, food riots spread across France, poachers defy the game laws, granaries are raided and towns raise their own militias.
A false rumor about wages targets Réveillon, a self-made wallpaper manufacturer in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine who backed the first balloon flights and paid workers well.
A crowd of thousands wrecks and burns Réveillon's house and workshop; troops fire, killing perhaps 300, the bloodiest day until 1792.
After the riot Paris is patrolled like an occupied city, with German and Hungarian regiments on its streets fuelling talk of a coup.
Via the Marquis de Ferrières, the hosts show how court dress for deputies, devised by young master of ceremonies Dreux-Brézé, stressed rank and invented tradition.
The royal procession through Versailles to the church of Saint-Louis displays the social hierarchy, with the Third Estate trailing behind in plain black.
r: e:n:opening procession of the estates general

g.u: Portrait of Mirabeau: scarred, scandalous noble and pornographer who attacked his own order, won a Third Estate seat for Aix and wanted British-style monarchy.
Other Third Estate figures, including Sieyès, Mounier and the young Robespierre, and why its lawyer-heavy membership was ambitious and resentful rather than popular.
At the opening session the Third Estate sits at the back, a hat-doffing muddle follows the king's speech, and Necker's long finance address bores everyone.
r: e:n:opening session of the estates general

g.u: When deputies are told to verify credentials by order, Mirabeau furiously refuses, setting the impassioned, Cicero-inspired tone of revolutionary oratory.
Politics borrows from popular theater: Parisians flock to the public galleries, and visiting Englishman Arthur Young is dismayed that spectators cheer and boo.
The deadlock drags on for a month while Mirabeau's printed reports to his constituents turn the assembly into a Paris media event.
Amid bleak reports and posters threatening revolt, Sieyès proposes an ultimatum on 10 June, and from 13 June parish priests begin to join the commons.
On 17 June, after rejecting clumsy alternatives, the deputies name themselves the National Assembly and claim sole authority over taxation.
Louis, already low, is shattered when his seven-year-old heir dies of tuberculosis on 4 June and withdraws to Marly to grieve.
r: e:n:death of the dauphin louis joseph

g.u: Necker urges concessions, the queen and royal brothers want a crackdown; Louis plans a royal session, and on 20 June deputies find their hall shut.
r: e:n:closure of the salle des menus-plaisirs

g.u: Guillotin finds a nearby real-tennis court where, at Mounier's urging and echoing David's Horatii, deputies swear not to part until France has a constitution.
At the royal session the Third Estate is kept waiting and Necker stays away; Louis concedes tax consent but rejects the National Assembly.
The Third Estate refuses to leave; Mirabeau tells Dreux-Brézé only bayonets will remove them, and Louis simply lets them stay.
Louis orders all three orders to join the Assembly; the royal family greets cheering crowds, Arthur Young declares the revolution complete, and Ferrières foresees bloodshed.
Foreign regiments march on Paris as the French Guards waver; hardliners urge sacking Necker, Broglie doubts the army, and some suggest retreating to Metz.
r: e:n:royal troop concentration around paris, july 1789

g.u: Late on 11 July Louis dismisses Necker and orders him out of France; a noble deputy warns his wife in Paris to stay in.
The hosts tease the fall of the Bastille in the next episode and sign off.

episodes.u: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook follow Paris from Necker's dismissal on 11 July 1789 through the riots, the hunt for weapons and the fall of the Bastille, contrasting the fortress's sinister legend with its rather comfortable reality. They then trace the aftermath: the killings of de Launay and Flesselles, the king's climbdown and visit to Paris under the new tricolour cockade, and the lynching of Foullon and Bertier a week later.

g.u: Recap of famine, royal debt and the Assembly's bid for sovereignty, with troops nearing Paris, bread prices doubling and talk of hidden enemies.
Louis XVI abruptly dismisses the popular finance minister Necker, who heads to Brussels yet still pledges his own fortune to guarantee food shipments.
On Sunday crowds pack the Palais-Royal, a pleasure quarter controlled by the Duke of Orléans, and learn at midday of Necker's fall.
Profile of Camille Desmoulins, a classics-obsessed young idealist and schoolfriend of Robespierre, likened to later generations of student radicals.
Desmoulins urges the crowd to arm and wear green leaves; marchers in mourning shut theatres and parade wax busts of Necker and Orléans.
r: e:n:desmoulins' call to arms at the palais-royal

g.u: German cavalry clash with protesters at Place Vendôme and the Tuileries; French Guards join the crowd and Besenval withdraws royal troops from Paris.
r: e:n:royal-allemand charge in the tuileries garden

g.u: Background on the customs wall ringing Paris, pushed by the tax farmer Lavoisier, whose pioneering chemistry and philanthropy complicate his reputation.
Rioters tear down the customs posts and burn their records overnight, as anxious propertied Parisians around Flesselles plan to summon the city's electors at dawn.
r: e:n:burning of the paris customs barriers

g.u: The tocsin spreads panic, Paris electors form a commune and a citizen militia, and swap Desmoulins' green for Paris's red and blue.
Looters raid the Saint-Lazare monastery for supposedly hoarded food, then seize antique arms, including a Siamese cannon, from a royal storehouse.
Flesselles sends arms-seekers on fruitless errands, fuelling suspicion; on 14 July a vast crowd storms the Invalides for muskets and cannon but finds no powder.
r: e:n:seizure of arms at the invalides

g.u: The real Bastille was a squat eight-towered fortress from the Hundred Years War, turned into a state prison under Charles VI and Richelieu.
How lettres de cachet allowed imprisonment without trial, and the Bastille's three kinds of inmates: alleged plotters, seditious writers, and unruly aristocratic sons.
Life inside the Bastille was surprisingly comfortable, with shops, gardens, books, billiards and fine meals that Marmontel fondly recalled, better than most French lives.
Linguet's lurid memoir fixes the Bastille's horror legend, the crown plans a monument in its place, and Sade's shouting gets him moved to Charenton.
Governor de Launay, a dutiful career official, guards 250 barrels of powder with elderly veterans, a few Swiss soldiers, scant food and no water.
Who the besiegers were: some 950 honoured victors, mostly migrant artisans from the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, plus one laundress, hungry and fearing the army.
City Hall envoys linger over a long meal with de Launay; Thuriot then demands the arms and powder, which the governor refuses without orders.
Impatient besiegers storm the outer courtyard, cut down a drawbridge that crushes one man, then come under fire and suspect a deliberate trap.
Hulin brings French Guards with cannon; de Launay threatens to blow the magazine, but his garrison objects and he surrenders by late afternoon.
Instead of martyrs the victors find just seven inmates, forgers, a libertine count and two madmen, and parade a bewildered bearded lunatic through Paris.
Revolutionary propaganda invents dungeons and torture devices, the ruins draw tourists, and contractor Palloy demolishes the fortress and sells souvenir relics across France.
The fate of the defenders: the Swiss escape by shedding uniforms, while the invalide Béquard, who prevented the explosion, is mutilated and later hanged.
Captured, de Launay is dragged to City Hall, killed by the mob and beheaded by the cook Desnot; suspected traitor Flesselles meets the same fate.
Rain calms Paris; at Versailles the Assembly reacts with alarm, the king's diary says nothing, and next day Louis pledges to withdraw troops.
r: e:n:louis xvi's address to the national assembly

g.u: An Assembly delegation led by Bailly and Lafayette reaches Paris; Bailly becomes mayor, Lafayette heads the militia and adds royal white to the cockade.
At a final royal council courtiers urge flight; the king stays, but Artois, the Polignacs and other princes leave, the first wave of émigrés.
Louis travels plainly to Paris, receives the city's keys from Bailly with a pointed Henry IV comparison, and accepts the tricolour cockade at City Hall.
Contemporaries hail the reconciliation as a world-historic example, and a bookseller predicts total renewal, introducing the universalist idealism of the Revolution.
A week later crowds lynch Foullon and his son-in-law Bertier de Sauvigny, killings Loustalot's paper defends, signalling that revolutionary violence has only begun.
r: e:n:lynching of foullon and bertier de sauvigny

g.u: The hosts sign off until the next episode.

episodes.yt: How One Night Swept Away 1,000 Years of Privilege
episodes.u: After the fall of the Bastille, the hosts follow the Great Fear in the countryside, the Night of 4 August that swept away feudal privilege, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. They then trace the Revolution's deepening rupture with the Catholic Church, from the seizure of Church lands to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and debate the Christian roots of revolutionary ideals.

g.u: Recap after the Bastille: a sovereign National Assembly, departing émigrés, a king recast as constitutional monarch, yet unresolved bread and money crises.
Why deputies debated a declaration of rights amid a food crisis: they judged that France's problems required a fresh constitutional order first.
As the Great Fear spreads, Arthur Young meets a prematurely aged peasant woman in Lorraine, while villagers storm châteaux and abbeys to burn feudal records.
Peasants level a Burgundy abbey tied to Talleyrand's family; the hosts profile Talleyrand, the lame, worldly Bishop of Autun who drafts rights texts with Mirabeau.
Rumours of aristocratic starvation plots and foreign-backed brigands spread panic; communities arm against imagined militias, foreigners and Jews are attacked, and deputies feel helpless.
On the evening of 4 August 1789 the Vicomte de Noailles, Lafayette's brother-in-law and Yorktown veteran, proposes ending feudal obligations and making everyone pay taxes.
Swept up in enthusiasm, clergy and nobles trade sacrifices, a bishop targeting hunting rights and a duke tithes, until privilege itself falls overnight.

Three weeks later comes Lafayette's American-inspired Declaration, its articles on equality, natural rights, national sovereignty, presumption of innocence, religious tolerance and free speech examined.
How original was the Declaration? The hosts see a world-historic break that still restates older ideas, caught between universal claims and emerging nationalism.
The Declaration dismantles the old order; noble titles and trappings vanish in June 1790, while the Church loses its tithes and religious monopoly.
Louis XVI's 1775 coronation at Reims, steeped in Clovis legends, dove-borne holy oil and an oath against heretics, binds the king to the Church.
Louis's tricolour cockade joins royal white to Paris's blue and red, the colours of Saints Martin and Denis, tying the new order to ancient legend.
r: e:n:louis xvi receives the tricolour cockade at the hôtel de ville

g.u: Did the Declaration break with Christian heritage or adapt it? The hosts introduce Jonathan Israel's radical Enlightenment, hostile to throne and altar, and Condorcet.
Comparing Condorcet's and Lavoisier's zeal for clean rivers to the modern anti-sewage campaigner Feargal Sharkey, the hosts joke about pollution and superstition.
Condorcet hails the Revolution as reason defeating superstition and hopes to purge France and the world of Christianity, which he blames for centuries of stagnation.
Voltaire, campaigner against the Church, made the 1762 execution of Toulouse Protestant Jean Calas a cause célèbre, winning the family royal reception and exoneration.
Talleyrand recalls meeting the aged Voltaire in Paris in 1778, and in 1791 revolutionaries rebury Voltaire's remains in the Panthéon as a founding inspiration.
r: e:n:transfer of voltaire's remains to the panthéon

g.u: Devout rural Catholics suspect a Protestant plot, pointing to Protestants' prominence in revolutionary bodies, including a pastor elected Assembly president in March 1790.
Reformation parallels: attacks on superstition, uncensored anticlerical pamphlets and prints, mock processions, parodies of the Mass and anticlerical plays in Paris theatres.
With France still bankrupt, Talleyrand proposes on 10 October 1789 seizing Church property and salarying clergy, echoing Henry VIII and Joseph II; the Assembly agrees.
Parish priests who first backed the Third Estate grow estranged, while monks and nuns lose everything as orders are dissolved in February 1790.
r: e:n:suppression of monastic orders in france (13 february 1790)

g.u: By summer 1790 clergy feel alienated: Talleyrand's Autun flock brands him a traitor, priests resist becoming civil servants, and Pius VI secretly condemns the reforms.
In July 1790 the Civil Constitution of the Clergy makes clergy elected, oath-bound state officials; historians call it the Revolution's decisive fracture.
Likened to a Brexit-style referendum, the clerical oath splits priests roughly 54 to 46, with Paris accepting and the west forming a counter-revolutionary bloc.
r: e:n:clerical oath to the civil constitution of the clergy

g.u: Le Barbier's 1789 painting of the Declaration, with broken chains, liberty cap, all-seeing eye and Mosaic stone tablets, raises whether Bible and Enlightenment could merge.
Tom roots Enlightenment values in Christianity, citing Calas's Christlike last words, his pardon on Christian grounds, and an archbishop's Pauline sermon for the Bastille dead.
Tom traces the Revolution to eleventh-century papal reform and twelfth-century Italian ideas of rights, framing its war on the Church as rival creeds colliding.
Louis XVI's September 1789 reply welcomes the Declaration's spirit but rejects its details, exposing the king as the missing piece in a British-style constitutional monarchy.
The hosts preview the next episode on the Women's March on Versailles and the Revolution's coming reckoning with the monarchy.

episodes.yt: The Day Versailles Fell to the People
episodes.u: The episode follows the autumn 1789 fights over the royal veto, bread shortages and Marat's journalism, up to the march of Paris market women and the National Guard on Versailles on 5-6 October. The royal family is forced back to the Tuileries, the Assembly follows them to Paris, and the Jacobin Club takes shape.

g.u: The October Days are introduced as the moment the royal family became prisoners of the Revolution, a bigger turning point for them than the Bastille.
Recap of the Bastille, the August decrees and the Declaration of Rights, plus the questions it left open on women, slavery and the monarchy.
Anglophile Paris nobles, tied by the hosts to Mirabeau, propose a British-style constitution with elected chamber, senate and royal veto; radical deputies reject any veto.
Sieyès condemns the plan as an attack on national sovereignty, and deputies begin sitting in rival blocs, giving politics its left and right.
r: e:n:division of the assembly into left and right

g.u: The Assembly throws out a second chamber and settles on a suspensive royal veto, a compromise the hosts compare to the 1911 Parliament Act.
Paris turns against the veto and a king who answers the August decrees and Declaration grudgingly, amid talk of moving the Assembly to Tours.
Despite a fine harvest, drought idles the water mills and bread prices climb again, feeding riots and rumours of an aristocratic plot to starve Paris.
With censorship gone, Jean-Paul Marat, a restless doctor and failed savant, launches L'Ami du peuple and fills it with tirades against hidden plotters.
Moderate admirers take fright at threats of lynching, an aborted August march on Versailles fizzles, and Palais-Royal radicals call for another.
Unable to control a free press, the revolutionaries set up a committee of inquiry with powers to open mail, spy and detain without trial.
r: e:n:creation of the comité des recherches

g.u: Lafayette struggles to keep order in Paris with the National Guard; the hosts disagree on whether he was indecisive or a decent moderate.
Reports reach Paris of a royal guards' banquet for the Flanders Regiment where the tricolour cockade was supposedly trampled with the queen's blessing.
At dawn on 5 October a market woman rouses others to march on Versailles, while the queen idles at Trianon and the king goes shooting.
Why these pastimes rankled: the Trianon idyll fed the queen's image, and the end of noble hunting rights set off a free-for-all of shooting.
Word of the march reaches the queen, reportedly via her hairdresser; Louis returns, his council weighs flight, and he blames Orléans.
Summoned by drum and bells, thousands of market women seize arms and cannon at the Hôtel de Ville and march on Versailles in the rain.
The poissardes traditionally brought the queen flowers each Saint Louis day, and Versailles entertainments mimicked their speech; now they loathe her but waver over Louis.
Men and soldiers of the Flanders Regiment join the swelling, festive procession, and the armed horsewoman Théroigne de Méricourt becomes its legendary emblem.
Some 15,000 National Guards insist on following the women, and a reluctant Lafayette rides at their head, carried along by his own men.
Repulsed at the palace, the soaked women invade the Assembly; their delegate Louison Chabry faints before Louis, who promises grain and accepts the decrees outright.
r: e:n:louis xvi's acceptance of the august decrees and the declaration

g.u: Lafayette reaches Versailles and trades a barb about Cromwell; the hosts argue over whether his refusal to grab power was weakness or virtue.
Lafayette, mud-spattered, urges Louis to send grain and move to Paris; the king stalls until morning, and Lafayette slips off near dawn to sleep.
At dawn the crowd breaks in and kills guards at the queen's door; Marie Antoinette escapes barefoot through a hidden passage to the king's rooms.
The hosts stress the savagery of the killings and how the queen's flight became an enduring conservative image, from Burke onward.
Lafayette wakes, calms the crowd, and brings Louis onto the balcony to agree to go to Paris, pinning a tricolour cockade on a royal bodyguard.
The terrified queen faces the hostile courtyard alone; Lafayette kisses her hand and the crowd's mood swings to cheers for her.
Led by the guards' heads on pikes, a seven-hour procession takes the silent royals to the Hôtel de Ville and the Tuileries, where Fersen waits.
The hosts weigh sympathy for the royals against the unrecorded starving, and British writers' habit of seeing the Revolution through Marie Antoinette.
After the October Days the Assembly strips the king of key powers, then itself moves to Paris, exposed to factions and pressure from the crowds.
r: e:n:curtailment of royal powers after the october days
e:n:transfer of the national constituent assembly to paris

g.u: The radical Breton Club follows to Paris, rents a room from the Dominicans and opens to paying citizens, becoming known as the Jacobins.
A Star Wars joke about the Jacobins, thanks to the producer, and a French sign-off.

episodes.yt: How a Tiny French Town Stopped Louis XVI Escaping France
episodes.u: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook survey radical Paris in late 1790 and the royal couple's growing estrangement from the revolution, then follow the June 1791 escape attempt in close detail. They trace how the family was recognized, halted at Varennes and escorted back to a silent Paris, and argue that a politicized countryside doomed both the plan and the monarchy.

g.u: The hosts preview a dramatic royal escape gamble, then recall how the October 1789 march brought the royal family to the Tuileries.
Paris in late 1790 buzzes with cockades, newspapers and patriotic songs, while Desmoulins and Marat push a populist message blaming hidden plotters.
Exhausted deputies, buried in correspondence while drafting a constitution, dwindle in attendance as nobles and clergy retreat home, leaving roughly 400 regulars in charge.
The Jacobin Club, decorated with busts of Brutus and Cato, spreads affiliates across France, while the radical Cordeliers Club on the Left Bank outflanks it.
Only tax-paying men count as active citizens; popular societies grow angrier as assignat printing fuels inflation and strikes sweep Paris, alarming the deputies.
Mirabeau cautions that ordinary people expect tangible improvement; compromised by secret payments from the court, he fades politically and dies in April 1791.
Barnave's moderates want a settlement with Louis, who looks cooperative after his plain-coated oath at the July 1790 Fête de la Fédération.
Writing to Spain's king, Louis secretly disowns his concessions; backed by Marie Antoinette, he is tormented when the Pope condemns the clerical oath.
The indecisive king finally asks for an escape plan toward loyal eastern garrisons, and Axel von Fersen devises it, visiting the Tuileries in disguise.
The hosts joke about a television detective series starring Fersen and the hairdresser Léonard, and pick actors to play them.
The escape party swells to eleven, including the children, Madame Élisabeth and nannies, so Fersen commissions a lavish, conspicuous berline coach.
Contrasting Louis with the cunning Charles II, who fled England incognito, the hosts argue the royals cannot imagine truly disguising themselves.
A crowd blocks the royals' Easter trip to Saint-Cloud for nearly two hours; Louis then feigns loyalty to the Assembly and plans a Montmédy route.
The plan's endgame is doubtful: troops are few, and Austrian envoy Mercy-Argenteau warns of civil war, yet the frightened couple will not wait.
On 20 June 1791 the royals act normally, but the children's attendants are dismissed and empty cabs wait on both sides of the Seine.
Louis drafts a declaration disowning his forced concessions, then says goodbye to his brother Provence, the future Louis XVIII, who flees separately to Brussels.
r: e:n:declaration of the king to all the french

g.u: Marie Antoinette and the governess Madame de Tourzel disguise the children, then use a secret key to slip them out among departing servants.
Fersen, disguised as a Paris cabman, drives the children around to pass time, while Lafayette and Mayor Bailly delay the king with a late visit.
Louis walks calmly out past the guards, Marie Antoinette narrowly avoids Lafayette, and Fersen drives the reunited family to the Saint-Martin barrier.
Running late, the family boards the berline; Fersen leaves them at Bondy for the Austrian Netherlands, and the nannies' coach joins at Claye.
Crossing Champagne at dawn, Louis tracks the route on his maps, plays the baroness's steward in the cover story, and relaxes, chatting with locals.
The bodyguards' yellow outfits recall the émigré Prince de Condé's livery, yet Louis shrugs off risk; he is recognized at Montmirail, Chaintrix and Châlons.
Nearing the Argonne, the royals miss Choiseul's cavalry escort, which hostile peasants had unsettled; Léonard tells other detachments to stand down.
At Sainte-Menehould postmaster Drouet recognizes the queen and the king from his face on paper money, and townsmen send him riding ahead to Varennes.
Outside Varennes the promised fresh horses are missing; Drouet gallops past them, rouses the town, and grocer-magistrate Sauce and the militia halt the coaches.
Unsure of the papers, officials lodge the travellers above Sauce's shop; judge Destez recognizes Louis, who embraces the councillors and pleads for their help.
Politicized by its Jacobin club and invasion fears, Varennes sounds the tocsin, militias pack the street, and officials insist the king return to Paris.
Couriers deliver the order to halt the king; Marie Antoinette flings it down, Louis resigns himself, and the coaches depart amid hostile crowds.
On the hot, dusty four-day return, crowds pelt the coach and revive old slanders, and peasants near Sainte-Menehould murder the royalist Count of Dampierre.
r: e:n:return of the royal family to paris
e:n:killing of the comte de dampierre

g.u: Three Assembly commissioners join the convoy; Barnave, seated beside Marie Antoinette, believes they can work together, a costly misjudgment for his Feuillant faction.
r: e:n:return of the royal family to paris

g.u: Paris greets the coach in enforced silence; at the Tuileries the crowd mauls the bodyguards, and Louis's widely read declaration exposes his duplicity.
r: e:n:return of the royal family to paris

g.u: The hosts judge the escape could have succeeded but failed mainly through Louis's long delay and his misreading of a provincial France transformed by revolution.
Closing the first run, the hosts promise an autumn return covering the monarchy's fall and the Terror, then preview Piltdown Man and Italian food episodes.
